title: Fed by ravens (1 Kings 17:1–7)
hook: Elijah hides by a brook, and ravens bring bread and meat

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehoboam, a young king who set aside the old men's counsel. Your line was listen to the old ones.

Bread and meat, twice a day, delivered by birds. But first a man walks into the story out of nowhere. No birth story, no call. Just a name, Elijah the Tishbite, of Gilead, and a sentence to Ahab, the king of Israel: "As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." Then, just as suddenly, the word comes to Elijah: get out of here. Turn east. Hide yourself by the brook Cherith, near the Jordan.

Here's the promise, in the King James Bible: "thou shalt drink of the brook; and I have commanded the ravens to feed thee there." He goes, and it happens: "the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook." Three things are worth slowing down for. First, the delivery service. In the law of Moses, the raven is on the list of birds Israel was not to eat: "Every raven after his kind." So the prophet's bread comes in the beak of a bird his own law kept off the table. Help from an unexpected quarter. Second, Elijah has to receive it. A man who has just faced down a king sits by a stream and waits for birds. There's no way to earn this meal, only to be there when it comes. Third, it doesn't last. "And it came to pass after a while, that the brook dried up, because there had been no rain in the land." The drought Elijah announced reaches him too. The ravens were for a season, not forever, and tomorrow's story begins because the water ran out. Much later, Jesus points at the same birds when he talks about worry. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Consider the ravens: for they neither sow nor reap; which neither have storehouse nor barn; and God feedeth them." Some readers hear the two passages together: the bird that is fed, and the bird that feeds a prophet.
screen: `AFTER A WHILE, THE BROOK DRIED UP.`

segments.voice: Think back to help you got from a source you'd never have chosen: a stranger, someone you didn't much like, a setback that turned out to carry something. Then ask whether help is being offered now that you've been too proud, or too wary, to take, and just picture receiving it. If you pray, give thanks for one raven in your life.
Cherith. The brook where Elijah hid in a drought, kept alive by ravens' bread and meat morning and evening, until the water ran out.
Your line: the ravens came. Bread and meat, morning and evening, from an unlikely beak. That's day seven hundred thirty.

howItsDone: Some Christians read Elijah and the ravens as a picture of God's daily provision, and the story is sometimes paired with Jesus's words about the ravens in Luke 12 when churches teach about worry.

chat.says: Why does the Elijah story make such a point of ravens feeding him?
options: Ravens were birds the law said not to eat, yet God sent help through them.
Ravens were sacred birds in Israel, kept near the altar for prayers.
Ravens were the only birds that could fly that far during a drought.
chat.meaning: In the law of Moses the raven was a bird not to eat, yet it carried Elijah's bread: help from an unexpected quarter.

Elijah.meaning: the prophet who announced the drought to King Ahab

Tishbite.meaning: a label the text gives Elijah, for where he came from

Ahab.meaning: king of Israel when Elijah announced the drought
